source.title: Conflicting Biases at the Edge of Stability: Norm versus Sharpness Regularization
source.authors: Vít Fojtík; M. Matveev; Hung-Hsu Chou; Gitta Kutyniok; Johannes Maly

record.file_problem: Full paper and supplement supplied; text is not visibly cut off or garbled in a way that prevents extraction.
record.tranche_reason: The paper sweeps learning rates and measures training loss and sharpness in full-batch gradient descent. Its experiments bear on the edge-of-stability behavior in V5 and report a limited batch-normalization convergence result relevant to V6, using different models and measures from the original sources.
record.gate_note: The paper does not report training classification error rates, random-label fitting, residual-versus-plain depth comparisons, initialization methods designed to preserve signals, or BN accuracy-speed comparisons. Cited prior-work results are not extracted as rows. Reported test-loss curves are outside the claim versions.
record.test_reason: The study directly reproduces the full-batch edge-of-stability component of V5 using training-loss trajectories and Hessian sharpness. Its baseline follows Cohen et al.'s experimental setup and builds on their code. It does not establish a controlled batch-normalization effect for V6.
record.authors_conclusion: The record is broadly accurate but omits the central conclusion: a single implicit bias is insufficient to explain generalization. Experiments show a learning-rate-controlled norm–sharpness trade-off, and simplified regression analysis shows that neither extreme necessarily generalizes best. Full-batch GD is the main systematic setting, with supplementary experiments using SGD, Shampoo, and Muon.
record.recipe_differences: The study examines learning-rate sweeps and sharpness–norm behavior, rather than the original claim's training-error comparisons or interventions. It primarily uses full-batch gradient descent and fixed training-loss thresholds.
record.method_sensitivity: Learning rate and its threshold relative to gradient-flow sharpness; training-loss threshold; initialization seed and scale; loss function; architecture and width; dataset size; parameterization. The authors report that CE can fail to converge even below 1/s0, increased initialization scale can cause instability or divergence, and increasing width alone on MNIST-5k can dissolve the increasing-norm trend.

fits_no_version.finding: A CNN with batch normalization converges at comparatively higher learning rates, but the comparison is unspecified and unmatched.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The tested BN CNN on CIFAR-10-5k reaches its CE training-loss target across the reported learning-rate range.

fits_no_version.finding: Increasing learning rate trades lower final sharpness against higher parameter norm, with intermediate rates sometimes giving the best generalization.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Learning rate controls a trade-off between implicit norm and sharpness biases, neither of which alone universally optimizes generalization.

record.peer_reviewed: Proceedings of the 43rd International Conference on Machine Learning, PMLR 306, 2026
record.problems: The paper's relevant training-dynamics findings are mostly qualitative; some outcomes are shown in figures. It reports limited full-dataset configurations, and the batch-normalization convergence statement lacks a clearly specified matched comparison. The study uses full-batch gradient descent.
record.rows_left_out: No additional claim-relevant rows identified. Figure-only curves are not assigned numeric values because the supplied text does not describe exact plotted values.

untested.parts: Training classification error and the specified SGD/Adam, random-label, model-size, early-stopping, and regularization comparisons.
Teacher-student ReLU local minima and extra student neurons.
Depth-dependent training degradation, matched identity-shortcut comparisons, very deep tanh initialization, and Fixup.
Activation-matched signal-preserving initialization, trainable depth, and orthogonal-versus-Gaussian training speed. Initialization-scale sweeps do not measure these claims.
The specified wide-network squared-loss catapult sequence relative to the initial linearized stability limit, including a brief initial loss rise followed by curvature reduction and recovery.
Matched BN-versus-no-BN accuracy-speed and learning-rate-tolerance effects, and Fixup.

missing.what: Separate CE trajectory result: progressive sharpening and oscillation around 2/η are followed by a substantial sharpness decline while training proceeds to a lower loss threshold.
Initialization-dependent failure: with 10× initialization, training diverges below ηc; maximum sharpness already occurs at initialization, making ηc the initial 2/s0 threshold.

CE training often fails to converge even below 1/s0, whereas MSE often converges at comparatively higher rates. Record failure to converge separately from proven divergence because the authors also describe stagnation.

record.verdict_notes: This study is not an original source for the versions. High-rate divergence is already allowed by V5 and does not itself warrant limits_scope. Missing BN controls and unmeasured accuracy speed are untested parts, not evidence limiting V6. Numerical figure values were not reconstructed from extracted axis text.

versions.untested_parts: Training classification error, random or corrupted labels, CIFAR-100, model size, early stopping, and regularized recipes.
Two-layer ReLU teacher-student local minima and the effect of extra student width.
Plain-versus-residual training error by depth, special initialization for very deep plain networks, and Fixup.
Activation-matched initialization, signal and gradient propagation, orthogonal versus Gaussian weights, and very deep plain convolutional training.

The paper measures edge-of-stability training dynamics, but does not report the specified wide-network squared-loss recovery-after-a-brief-rise result or a systematic stability-limit sweep in terms of an initial linearized model. Its relevant findings are mainly qualitative and aggregate across configurations.

The paper reports that a CNN with batch normalization converges at comparably higher learning rates, but does not report faster accuracy gain or a controlled comparison with the same network without normalization. Fixup is not tested.

rows.subject: FCN and other tested configurations (aggregate as described by the authors)
rows.size_stated: Compact models; base FCN has two hidden layers with 200 neurons each
rows.operation_detail: Full-batch gradient descent over learning rates; training stopped at a fixed loss threshold

conditions.value: MNIST and CIFAR-10; configurations also vary architecture, activation, loss, initialization, and loss threshold

rows.measure: Training-loss behavior and loss sharpness during training
rows.value: In EoS, loss decreases on average non-monotonically and sharpness fluctuates just above 2/η; some configurations diverge at high learning rates
rows.note: Aggregate qualitative description across configurations; the paper does not give a per-model numeric loss-rise-and-recovery result matching V5.
rows.check: The reported non-monotone loss decrease and sharpness oscillations around 2/η directly exhibit V5's full-batch component; untested catapult details do not make this partial. Split this aggregate into ordinary-initialization EoS trajectories, CE trajectories with subsequent sharpness decline, and initialization-dependent failures. Figure 14 and Section I.11 provide direct trajectory evidence. The threshold 2/sGF uses maximum gradient-flow trajectory sharpness, not necessarily initial sharpness or an initial linearized model.

source_check.problem: The qualitative EoS result is supported, but Figure 17 concerns a two-dimensional diagonal linear network rather than the aggregate FCN result.

rows.subject: CNN with Batch Normalization
rows.size_stated: Two convolutional layers with 32 filters each; size otherwise not stated
rows.operation_detail: Full-batch gradient descent across learning rates
rows.value: Comparably higher learning rates still converge
rows.note: The text does not identify the comparison set for “comparably higher,” and this does not measure accuracy gain or compare against the same network without batch normalization.
rows.check: Convergence of a BN CNN at unspecified comparatively higher learning rates does not establish BN's effect relative to the same network without BN. The supplied experiments lack a matched no-BN CIFAR-10 comparison and an accuracy-speed comparison.
